Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

bind verb

by a promise, an oath or a kindness

also oblige, put under an obligation, be bound, bound by, binding

classical

Cic. Leg. 2.41: vōtī spōnsiō, quā obligāmur deō (Lewis & Short)
Plin. Ep. 4.4.2: obligābis mē (Lewis & Short)

obligō, obligāre, obligāvī, obligātum

verb, first conjugation: the person in the accusative, the bond in the ablative, the person bound to in the dative

bind, oblige, put under an obligation

Bind by a vow, an oath, a contract or a kindness: obligātus eī nihil eram, “I owed him nothing” (Cic. Fam. 6.11.1, Lewis & Short). Literally “tie up, bandage” (rare); it also means “pledge, mortgage” and, with a crime, “make guilty of” (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • obstringō, obstringere, obstrīnxī, obstrictum — bind, lay under an obligation

    verb, third conjugation: the person in the accusative, the bond in the ablative · also used · classical · Caes. BG 1.9: quam plūrimās cīvitātēs suō sibi beneficiō habēre obstrictās volēbat (Lewis & Short); Caes. BG 1.31; Tac. A. 1.14, of binding by an oath (Lewis & Short)

    The classical sense of the word (Lewis & Short): bind by an oath, a law, a kindness or a debt (aere aliēnō, Cic. Fam. 11.10.5). With sē and a crime it is “make oneself guilty of”; literally “tie up” (Plautus), rare.

Examples

  • prīncipēs sint patria et parentēs, quōrum beneficiīs maximīs obligātī sumus

    first should come our country and our parents, to whom we are bound by the greatest kindnessesCic. Off. 1.58

  • gaudent mūneribus, sed nec data imputant nec acceptīs obligantur

    they love gifts, but they neither count what they give nor feel bound by what they receiveTac. Germ. 21.3

  • quam plūrimās cīvitātēs suō sibi beneficiō habēre obstrictās volēbat

    he wanted to have as many states as possible bound to him by his own kindnessCaes. BG 1.9 (Lewis & Short)

See also promise, word, tie.

SourcesLewis & Short: obligo · Lewis & Short: obstringo
